q: What is a knowledge audit?
r: A review of what knowledge an organization has and where gaps exist
It guides what to capture or build.
w: A review of a firm's yearly tax payments to the government
A review of the number of computers in the office
A review of customers' complaints about product prices

q: A company learns that only one employee knows how to run a key machine. What should it do?
r: Document the process and train a second person
Sharing reduces dependence on one worker.
w: Keep the process secret to protect the worker's job
Wait until the worker leaves before acting
Ban anyone else from touching the machine

q: What is institutional memory?
r: The shared knowledge and history an organization holds over time
Policies and experience form part of it.
w: The computer storage in a company server room
A list of past customers' addresses

q: What is a document management system?
r: Software that stores, organizes and controls access to documents
Versions and permissions are tracked.
w: A machine that prints documents faster
A rule that bans paper in an office
A tool that sets employee schedules

q: Why is version control useful for shared documents?
r: It shows which version is current and lets teams recover earlier ones
Confusion and overwriting are reduced.
w: It makes documents impossible to edit
It deletes all earlier versions automatically

q: What is a frequently asked questions (FAQ) page for?
r: Answering common questions so people can find help quickly
It saves staff time.

q: What is training documentation?
r: Written guides that teach employees how to do tasks
It supports consistent learning.
w: A list of tasks employees must avoid
A report of the firm's yearly profit

q: New hires keep asking the same setup questions. What is the best long-term fix?
r: Create a clear onboarding guide that answers them
One resource replaces repeated explanations.
w: Tell them to stop asking questions
That does not solve the problem.

q: What is a data governance policy?
r: Rules for how an organization collects, stores and uses data
It protects accuracy and privacy.
w: A rule that sets product prices
A schedule of backup tapes only
A list of the firm's competitors

q: What is job shadowing as a way to share knowledge?
r: Following an experienced worker to learn how tasks are done
Learners see real practice.
w: Replacing a worker for a week with no guidance
Reading a manual alone with no practice
Watching a video of an unrelated industry

q: Which method best passes on skills that are hard to write down?
r: Mentoring and working side by side
Tacit knowledge transfers through practice.
w: Emailing a long list of rules
Posting a single notice on a wall

q: What does it mean to curate information?
r: To select, organize and keep the most useful and accurate material
Quality matters more than volume.
w: To collect every document without checking it
To hide information from all staff

q: A shared drive has thousands of outdated, duplicate files. What is the best response?
r: Review, organize and remove or archive outdated files
A clean system is easier to use.
w: Tell staff to avoid the drive
Delete every file at once without checking

q: What is a quality circle?
r: A small group of employees who meet to solve work quality problems
They suggest improvements.
w: A group of customers who test prices
That is not a quality circle.
A circle drawn on a chart of sales
A meeting held to assign blame

q: Workers on a line meet weekly to find ways to cut defects. What is this?
r: A quality circle
Employees address quality problems together.
w: No tax on imports is shown.

q: What is a control chart used for?
r: Tracking a process over time to spot changes that signal problems
It shows when a process drifts.
w: Choosing the color of a product
Setting the price of a product

q: What is a Pareto chart based on?
r: The idea that a few causes produce most of the problems
The 80/20 rule is an example.
w: The idea that all causes are equally important
The idea that problems solve themselves
The idea that price decides quality

q: A review shows two causes account for 80 percent of defects. What should the team do first?
r: Focus on fixing those two causes
Fixing the biggest causes has the largest effect.
w: Spread effort equally across all causes
Ignore both and fix the smallest cause

q: What is a fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram used for?
r: Organizing possible causes of a problem to find the root cause
Teams group causes by category.
w: Showing a company's profit by month
Mapping the path of a delivery truck
Listing the steps of a sale

q: What is a customer requirement in quality management?
r: A need or expectation a product or service must satisfy
Quality means meeting them.
w: A rule that customers must follow in a store
A fee customers pay for service

q: Customers say a fitness app crashes too often. Which quality step comes first?
r: Measure the crashes and find their cause
Data guides the fix.
w: Raise the price of the app
Hide the complaints from the team

q: What is a service guarantee?
r: A promise to fix or refund if a service does not meet stated standards
It builds trust.
w: That is a menu of services.

q: A delivery firm promises a refund if a package is more than a day late. What is this?
r: A service guarantee
It sets a clear standard and remedy.

q: What is a quality management system (QMS)?
r: A set of processes and rules for meeting quality goals consistently
ISO 9001 describes one.

q: Why do many firms train all employees in quality methods?
r: Quality depends on everyone, not just inspectors
Prevention starts with each worker.
w: Training removes the need for any standards
Training makes products cost more by law

q: What is supplier quality management?
r: Working with suppliers to ensure inputs meet quality standards
Poor inputs lead to poor products.

q: A bakery's flour supplier ships low-quality flour and cakes fail. What is the best response?
r: Set quality requirements and review the supplier's performance
Inputs affect final quality.
w: Keep buying the same flour without changes

q: What is a risk register?
r: A list of identified risks with their likelihood, impact and plans
Managers use it to track risks.
w: A list of customers who pay late
A list of employees' vacation days
A list of products on sale

q: A project team lists possible problems, rates each and assigns an owner. What is this?
r: Maintaining a risk register
Risks are recorded and tracked.

q: What is risk probability?
r: The chance that a risk event will happen
It is part of assessing a risk.
w: The cost of fixing a risk
The date a risk was listed
The person responsible for a risk

q: What is risk impact?
r: The size of the loss or harm if a risk event happens
High impact means serious consequences.
w: The chance that the event will occur
The name of the person who found the risk
The list of insurance policies owned

q: A risk has low probability but very high impact, such as a factory fire. How is it usually managed?
r: With insurance and prevention measures
High-impact risks deserve protection.
w: It is ignored because it is unlikely
It is accepted with no plan
It is avoided by closing the business

q: What is a business continuity plan?
r: A plan for keeping key operations running during a crisis
It prepares for disruptions.
w: A plan to raise prices every year
A plan to change the company's logo
A plan to hire more staff in summer

q: A store keeps off-site backups of records and a backup power source. What is this?
r: Business continuity planning
It protects operations during disruption.

q: What is a disaster recovery plan?
r: Steps to restore systems and data after a major disruption
It limits downtime.
w: Steps to start a new product
Steps to lower the price of goods

q: What is workplace safety training?
r: Teaching employees how to avoid accidents and respond to hazards
It reduces injuries.

q: After several slips on a wet floor, which step best reduces the risk?
r: Fix the leak, post warnings and clean spills promptly
It removes the hazard and warns people.

q: What is a supply chain risk?
r: The chance that a disruption in the supply chain will hurt the business
Late shipments are an example.
w: The chance that a customer will leave a review
That is not a supply risk.
The chance that a logo will be redesigned
That is not a supply risk.
The chance that a sale will be announced
That is not a supply risk.

q: A company relies on one overseas supplier and a port strike halts shipments. Which step reduces this risk in future?
r: Adding backup suppliers in other regions
Diversifying sources reduces dependence.
w: Relying more on the same supplier

q: What is credit risk for a business?
r: The chance that a customer will not pay what they owe
Late or unpaid invoices create it.
w: The chance that a product will be returned
The chance that a store will run out of stock
The chance that an employee will resign

q: A firm checks a new customer's payment history before offering credit terms. What is this?
r: Managing credit risk
It lowers the chance of unpaid bills.

q: What is reputational risk?
r: The chance that damage to a company's image will hurt its business
Scandals and poor service can cause it.
w: The chance that a machine will break
The chance that a delivery will arrive early
The chance that prices will fall by law

q: A company hides a product safety problem and customers find out. What is the likely result?
r: Serious damage to reputation and trust
Hiding problems makes harm worse.

q: What is a general journal?
r: A record where transactions are first written in order by date
Entries are later posted to the ledger.
w: A summary of a company's assets

q: A business buys supplies for cash. Which accounts are affected?
r: Supplies increase and Cash decreases
One asset replaces another.
w: Supplies increase and Accounts Payable decreases

q: What is a source document?
r: Evidence of a transaction, such as a receipt or invoice
It supports journal entries.
w: A summary of a company's yearly results
A list of the company's accounts
That is a chart of accounts.

q: What is a chart of accounts?
r: A list of the accounts a business uses to record transactions
Each account has a name and number.
w: A graph of sales over time
A list of customers and their balances

q: Account numbers beginning with 1 usually stand for which type of account?
r: Assets
The usual order is assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses.

q: What is a bank reconciliation?
r: Comparing a company's cash records with the bank statement
It explains differences between them.
w: Combining two bank accounts into one

q: Which item is subtracted from the bank statement balance in a bank reconciliation?
r: Outstanding checks
The bank has not yet paid them.

q: What is a petty cash fund?
r: A small amount of cash kept for minor expenses
Receipts support spending.
w: A large fund for buying equipment

q: What is an invoice?
r: A bill that lists goods or services sold and the amount due
The seller sends it to the buyer.
w: A receipt for a cash sale

q: What does the term 2/10, net 30 on an invoice mean?
r: A 2 percent discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise full in 30
It rewards early payment.
w: A 10 percent discount if paid within 2 days
Payment is due in 2 or 10 days
It is a discount, not a fee.

q: What is payroll?
r: The process of paying employees and withholding taxes
It includes records of hours and deductions.

q: An employee earns $1,500 gross with $225 withheld for taxes. What is net pay?
What is the purpose of financial software such as accounting packages?
r: Recording transactions and producing reports automatically
It saves time and reduces errors.
